entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17595"/><div sID="gen35449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17595"/><hi type="bold">2. the course of this world--</hi>the career (literally, "the age," compare <reference osisRef="Gal.1.4">Ga 1:4</reference>), or present system of this world (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">3:18</reference>, 19, as opposed to "the world to come"): alien from God, and lying in the wicked one (<reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1Jo 5:19</reference>). "The age" (which is something more external and ethical) regulates "the world" (which is something more external).<div eID="gen35449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prince of the power of the air--</hi>the unseen God who lies underneath guiding "the course of this world" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>); ranging through the air around us: compare <reference osisRef="Mark.4.4">Mr 4:4</reference>, "fowls of the air" (Greek, "heaven") that is, (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>), "Satan" and his demons. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>. Christ's ascension seems to have cast Satan out of heaven (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.5">Re 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.9.10">9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.13">12, 13</reference>), where he had been heretofore the accuser of the brethren (<reference osisRef="Job.1.6-Job.1.11">Job 1:6-11</reference>). No longer able to accuse in heaven those justified by Christ, the ascended Saviour (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.33">Ro 8:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">34</reference>), he assails them on earth with all trials and temptations; and "we live in an atmosphere poisonous and impregnated with deadly elements. But a mighty purification of the air will be effected by Christ's coming" [Auberlen], for Satan shall be bound (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.12">Re 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">13, 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.2">20:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">3</reference>). "The power" is here used collectively for the "powers of the air"; in apposition with which "powers" stand the "spirits," comprehended in the singular, "the spirit," taken also collectively: the aggregate of the "seducing spirits" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>) which "work now (still; not merely, as in your case, 'in time past') in the sons of disobedience" (a Hebraism: men who are not merely by accident disobedient, but who are essentially sons of disobedience itself: compare <reference osisRef="Matt.3.7">Mt 3:7</reference>), and of which Satan is here declared to be "the prince." The Greek does not allow "the spirit" to refer to Satan, "the prince" himself, but to "the powers of the air" of which he is prince. The powers of the air are the embodiment of that evil "spirit" which is the ruling principle of unbelievers, especially the heathen (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Ac 26:18</reference>), as opposed to the spirit of the children of God (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.33">Lu 4:33</reference>). The potency of that "spirit" is shown in the "disobedience" of the former. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.32.20">De 32:20</reference>, "children in whom is no faith" (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.9">Is 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.4">57:4</reference>). They disobey the Gospel both in faith and practice (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2Th 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen35450" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17605"/><div sID="gen35485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17605"/><hi type="bold">12. without Christ--</hi>Greek, "separate from Christ"; having no part in Him; far from Him. A different Greek word (aneu) would be required to express, "Christ was not present with you" [Tittmann].<div eID="gen35485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">aliens--</hi>Greek, "alienated from," not merely "separated from." The Israelites were cut off from the commonwealth of God, but it was as being self-righteous, indolent, and unworthy, not as aliens and strangers [Chrysostom]. The expression, "alienated from," takes it for granted that the Gentiles, before they had apostatized from the primitive truth, had been sharers in light and life (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.23">23</reference>). The hope of redemption through the Messiah, on their subsequent apostasy, was embodied into a definite "commonwealth" or polity, namely, that "of Israel," from which the Gentiles were alienated. Contrast <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">Ep 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.4">4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.5">5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.147.20">Psa 147:20</reference>.<div eID="gen35486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covenants of promise--</hi>rather, "... of the promise," namely, "to thee and thy seed will I give this land" (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Ro 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Ga 3:16</reference>). The plural implies the several renewals of the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and with the whole people at Sinai [Alford]. "The promise" is singular, to signify that the covenant, in reality, and substantially, is one and the same at all times, but only different in its accidents and external circumstances (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">He 1:1</reference>, "at sundry times and in divers manners").<div eID="gen35487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having no ... hope--</hi>beyond this life (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.19">1Co 15:19</reference>). The CONJECTURES of heathen philosophers as to a future life were at best vague and utterly unsatisfactory. They had no divine "promise," and therefore no sure ground of "hope." Epicurus and Aristotle did not believe in it at all. The Platonists believed the soul passed through perpetual changes, now happy, and then again miserable; the Stoics, that it existed no longer than till the time of the general burning up of all things.<div eID="gen35488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without God--</hi>Greek, "atheists," that is, they had not "God" in the sense we use the word, the Eternal Being who made and governs all things (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.14.15">Ac 14:15</reference>, "Turn from these vanities unto the living God who made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things therein"), whereas the Jews had distinct ideas of God and immortality. Compare also <reference osisRef="Gal.4.8">Ga 4:8</reference>, "Ye knew not God ... ye did service unto them which are no gods" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.5">1Th 4:5</reference>). Translate, "For it is through Him (<reference osisRef="John.14.6">Joh 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">He 10:19</reference>) that we have our access (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.12">Ep 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Ro 5:2</reference>), both of us, in (that is, united in, that is, "by," <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.13">1Co 12:13</reference>, Greek) one Spirit to the Father," namely, as our common Father, reconciled to both alike; whence flows the removal of all separation between Jew and Gentile. Translate as Greek, "Built up upon," &c. (participle; having been built up upon; omit, therefore, "and are"). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">12</reference>. The same image in <reference osisRef="Eph.3.18">Ep 3:18</reference>, recurs in his address to the Ephesian elders (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Ac 20:32</reference>), and in his Epistle to Timothy at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>), naturally suggested by the splendid architecture of Diana's temple; the glory of the Christian temple is eternal and real, not mere idolatrous gaud. Christ Himself, the only true Foundation, was the grand subject of their ministry, and spring of their life. As one with Him and His fellow workers, they, too, in a secondary sense, are called "foundations" (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference>). The "prophets" are joined with them closely; for the expression is here not "foundations of the apostles and the prophets," but "foundations of the apostles and prophets." For the doctrine of both was essentially one (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1Pe 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>). The apostles take the precedency (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.24">Lu 10:24</reference>). Thus he appropriately shows regard to the claims of the Jews and Gentiles: "the prophets" representing the old Jewish dispensation, "the apostles" the new. The "prophets" of the new also are included. Bengel and Alford refer the meaning solely to these (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Ep 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">4:11</reference>). These passages imply, I think, that the New Testament prophets are not excluded; but the apostle's plain reference to <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>, "the head stone of the corner," proves that the Old Testament prophets are a prominent thought. David is called a "prophet" in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>. Compare also <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>; another prophet present to the mind of Paul, which prophecy leans on the earlier one of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>). The sense of the context, too, suits this: Ye were once aliens from the commonwealth of Israel (in the time of her Old Testament prophets), but now ye are members of the true Israel, built upon the foundation of her New Testament apostles and Old Testament prophets. Paul continually identifies his teaching with that of Israel's old prophets (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.22">Ac 26:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.23">28:23</reference>). The costly foundation-stones of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.17">1Ki 5:17</reference>) typified the same truth (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.26">Jr 51:26</reference>). The same stone is at once the corner-stone and the foundation-stone on which the whole building rests. Paul supposes a stone or rock so large and so fashioned as to be both at once; supporting the whole as the foundation, and in part rising up at the extremities, so as to admit of the side walls meeting in it, and being united in it as the corner-stone [Zanchius]. As the corner-stone, it is conspicuous, as was Christ (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1Pe 2:6</reference>), and coming in men's way may be stumbled over, as the Jews did at Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">Mt 21:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>). <div eID="gen35515" type="x-p"/>
